turn_text: Do you feel that there are adequate resources in the funding for the Department of Agriculture to implement this new Farm Bill?

Absolutely, and we put an additional $30 million in there to assist in the implementation of the Farm Bill. That I think the Department is happy for, the Secretary of Expressed Appreciation. But we want to see that work well, and we want to see them be able to deliver the services because our farmers have been stressed. They've been stressed with natural disasters, with low commodity prices, with the tariff wars, and they need to make sure that they have the full service of the Department of Agriculture. We also put a prohibition in the bill to stop the department from closing into the local farm service agency office because we want to make sure that there is excellent and efficient customer service for our farmers and our ranchers.

With regard to the trade wars, this administration has announced another round of market facilitation program payments to the tune of about $16 billion. But as was said by ranking member of the Senate ad committee, Senator Debbie Stabenow, the CCC has less than that amount in it. Are there funds here that would recycle that program or some additional appropriation to help the administration to follow through?

Well, a large part of that CCC funding comes from other sources rather than direct appropriations. And of course, the farmers are in great need of that funding to deal with the tariff force. And it's well received and will be well received by them because right now they're stressed. They're coming right off of the natural disasters and just not getting the disaster payments out of the door. They need to have something to tie them over.

The White House has been threatening already to veto this bill, saying it goes beyond spending that they had envisioned and funds programs that they didn't necessarily agree with. Have you been in communication with the White House about this and any idea of the direction that the Senate might take?

Well, what we have done is we received the statement of administration policy of where they didn't like the fact that we rejected that drastic cuts a lot of problems, a lot of the programs. However, it was on a bipartisan basis, particularly in our agriculture bill, that both sides of the aisle agreed that we should not be reducing the help to rule America and we shouldn't be cutting the water and waste water programs. We should not be reducing in the programs that the, for example, the international food programs, food for peace, the McGovern-Dole. On a bipartisan basis, we actually rejected the cuts. They had eliminated them. We funded it with increases. And that was a bipartisan decision. The rural communities were cut with the Rural Development Program through our housing. The only thing that the administration was pushing was broadband, and that was to that credit, but even that was less than what is needed. Of course, they were opposing to attack vulnerable populations, and of course, we didn't go along with that. So I think that because our bill is far-reaching and it touches every citizen every day with food safety, medicine safety, agricultural research, rural development, and the nutrition assistance. When the administration proposed to cut these things, people recognized that it just was not realistic and did not go along with it. And I think that I have to salute my colleagues on the other side of the aisle who who joined with us in saying, no, these programs need to be maintained.

turn_text: Mr. Chairman, Ag Secretary Purdue has begun the process of moving the ERS and the NIFA to Kansas City. We had a communication from thousands of scientists from hundreds of agriculture deans from the scientific community, from the research community, the statistical community, the various associations, all thinking that this is not a good idea and setting for very, very sound reasons. turn_text: Well We in the House can only do what we can do. And I think that we are giving good account for our stewardship and the ball now goes to the Senate and they will have to discharge their responsibilities. And of course, once that is done in communication and in cooperation with the administration, hopefully we'll do what we Constitutionally required to do and have a budget and have an appropriations bill by the September 30th deadline.
You think there's a chance we'll see a continuing resolution?

There's always a chance. In fact, there's a very high chance. But we're doing our debt level best to make sure that we don't have to have a continuing resolution that we can have appropriations bills passed in regular order.

Mr. Chairman, last week on this program we had Iowa Senator Johnny Arts to clearly talk about the devastation that had come to her region from the flooding this year. Your area is well familiar with natural disasters and, of course, the wildfires that took place on the West Coast. A three-billion-dollar disaster assistance bill was a long time coming. Mr. Ernst suggested that was probably a down payment for the loss that had been seen in her area, further loss still being seen with flooding along the major tributaries. And of course, your areas is clearly not back to normal following the disasters. Do you think there's a call from the countryside to come back for some additional funds to help these rural areas get back on their feet?

Without the shadow of a doubt, there was no way that we could allocate sufficient resources to deal with the floods that occurred after we had developed the disaster bill but prior to passage because the extent of the damage was not yet fully accounted for. We fully expect to have to have another supplemental to deal with the Midwestern flooding because the extent of that damage is yet to be fully determined. However, I'm hoping that we can do it with dispatch because I would hate for the people in the Midwest to have to go through the agony and the stress that people in the South Florida and Georgia and up the East Coast as a result of Hurricane Michael. Our disaster hit us in October. And of course, it was all the way until just a few weeks ago that we were finally able to get the disaster bill passed. So I hope that the Midwest doesn't have to go through that. I hope that we can get us supplemental once we get the damage assessments and that we can try to respond So that we can remediate what is taking place there.

Congressman Bishop, just a couple of questions left here and I would lead with this as a general question overall. The USMCA is waiting in the sidelines for the US perhaps to consider before the Congress and of course the president continues to work and to negotiate with China and a long trade war and there is talk of an agreement with the Japanese particularly on agriculture that could come quickly. How do you see this administration's work on trade and is there particular counsel that you might offer to this administration?

My counsel would be to trade very carefully and to be very cautious because I think the precipitous way that in which the negotiations have been conducted has created a great deal of confusion, a great deal of uncertainty, and I think that many, many people, particularly in the agriculture community, are very stressed because they don't know what the outcome is going to be. Many of them are hopeful that it will work out for the good in the long run, but they're feeling a lot of pain now, particularly some of the farmers in Iowa have been speaking out. They've been crying out with the pain and wondering how long will they have to suffer. So I'm not sure how well the trade negotiations are going. The agreement that the president's working on with Mexico and Canada will have winners and will have losers. There will be some segments of the American economy that will benefit and there will be other segments that will be disadvantaged. So we won't know really until we actually see it and can look at the details. As they say, the devil is always in the details.

You are identified as a blue dog Democrat. How does a blue dog with a moderate mindset toward budget and toward the country? How do you survive in this day? And can you find other partners to work with in this political climate?

Oh, absolutely. We have 27 blue dogs this year. We were in the teens last year, so we increased our numbers. As a matter of fact, the Democrat majority was gained not by progressives, but by members who replaced Republicans in marginal seats. So I think that somehow the loud voices have tended to dominate the media, but the Democratic Party, I think, is a broad enough tent that it can accommodate the full spectrum of views, political views in the country.
Chairman Bishop, I want to thank you so much for taking time out of your schedule to visit with us here on Open Mike. It is Open Mike, and the tradition is that you have the last word, sir.

Well, I'd just like to thank you for what you do in disseminating information to your audience, particularly the agriculture community. They search for it because they want to know that we are in Washington working for and in their beheld. And I certainly want to utilize my position as a member of Congress, as chairman of the Agriculture, Rural Development, FDA-related agencies, subcommittee appropriations to really utilize this position and this process to enhance the quality of life of people in rural America and to make sure that we in America can continue to boost the highest quality, the safest and most abundant and the most economical food and fiber anywhere in the world. We're doing that now and I'm going to do my dead level best to make sure that we're able to and that the American farmers and ranchers are able to do that for years to come.
